To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there was little evidence of statistically significant variance between wards in the prevalence of common mental disorders, which ranged from a low of 18.8 percent to a high of 29.5 percent, and associations between common mental disorders and characteristics of wards such as the Carstair’s index were only statistically significant among those who were not in paid employment.
there was little evidence that the prevalence of CMD varied across areas in England, Wales and Scotland.
the prevalence of common mental disorders ( CMD ) in Britain is not associated with area level characteristics of the places where people live.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the physical and social environment of the place where people live.

the extent to which the common mental disorders ( CMD ) in Britain are related to characteristics of the places where people live, and whether the effects of place are greatest among the economically inactive.

the extent to which the prevalence of the common mental disorders (depression, anxiety, and somatic symptoms) varies between areas, and whether this variation is related to area level socioeconomic characteristics, population density, and the ONS classification of wards.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of socioeconomic factors on the common mental disorders are complex and not easily summarised.
the effects of place of living are greatest among those not employed and that these effects may be due to a variety of factors.

there is no evidence of a significant urban-rural or socioeconomic gradient in CMD after adjusting for the characteristics of individual respondents, but there is some evidence of a significant gradient in those who are economically in active.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of place of living on mental health are greater for those who are more likely to spend more time at home, and that these effects are mediated by social capital.
the effects of neighbourhood on mental health are complex and depend on individual characteristics.
we have not found any evidence of an effect of area of residence on the prevalence of CMD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a significant urban-rural divide in the prevalence of the common mental disorders, which is not explained by the socioeconomic characteristics of the population.
the effects of socioeconomic inequalities are greatest on people who are not economically active.
the effects of socioeconomic inequalities on mental health are not simply a result of differences in the distribution of risk factors between socioeconomic groups.
